name: The Scorecard Publisher
oneLiner: Merges two disjoint eval pipelines — guardrail/contract probes and answer-quality grading — into one scorecard with a single Pass/Warning/Fail verdict and prioritized fixes.
lead: Two eval pipelines produce differently-shaped result files: contract/probe runs that assert the assistant obeys its rules and refuses bad requests, and quality-grading runs that score answer quality. This agent discovers the newest file from each, normalizes both into one summary (pass rate, verdict counts, gate failures, average scores), computes an overall verdict under fixed precedence rules, and emits a report with ranked, actionable recommendations.
chore: The manual path: open several raw result JSONs, read numbers out of each, decide by hand whether the whole run passes, and hand-write a summary for stakeholders who won't read raw data. Tedious, and easy to miss a critical failure buried in one pile.
instead: One scorecard that aggregates both pipelines, decides the overall verdict by explicit precedence, and lists — ranked by severity — what to fix and why.
whyItMatters: A single PII leak or a hallucinated answer can sink trust in the whole assistant. Surfacing gate failures first, and letting them override otherwise-green scores, is what keeps a launch honest.

howItWorks.step: Scans each result directory for files matching a naming pattern and picks the one with the newest mtime — so the scorecard always reflects the latest run of each pipeline, not a stale artifact.
howItWorks.explain: Uses filesystem `mtimeMs` — not filename ordering — as the recency key, because timestamped names don't sort lexically the way you'd expect. A **missing directory returns `undefined` rather than throwing**, so a pipeline that never ran is treated as 'nothing to merge' instead of a crash. The `pattern.test(f)` filter is what keeps sibling artifacts (logs, a stray `.docx`) out of the candidate set, and the descending `sort` means `files[0]` is always the newest — so the scorecard reflects the **latest run of each pipeline, never a stale artifact**.

howItWorks.step: Normalizes the two differently-shaped result files into one `EvalReportSummary` — pass rate, verdict counts, gate failures, average scores — so downstream code never branches on which pipeline a number came from.
howItWorks.explain: The whole point is **shape normalization**: two files with different schemas become one `EvalReportSummary` where each half is independently nullable, so a `--system-only` run leaves `userPrompt` null rather than fabricating zeros. The `|| { PASS: 0, ... }` and `|| { pii: 0, ... }` defaults are load-bearing — `computeOverallVerdict` later reads `gateFails.pii` and `verdicts.FAIL` unconditionally, so an omitted field in the raw JSON would throw without them. `recommendations` ships empty here and is filled by a **separate pass**, and the overall verdict is computed once, centrally, from the merged shape rather than trusted from either source file.

howItWorks.step: Computes one overall verdict by fixed precedence: any contract probe failure or any PII/safety gate failure forces FAIL, regardless of how high the quality scores are; only when nothing critical trips does it fall back to the weighted aggregate score.
howItWorks.explain: This is **precedence, not a rollup** — the checks run top-down and the first match returns, so `gateFails.pii > 0` forces `FAIL` before the quality `aggregate` is ever consulted; a green scorecard can never mask a leak. `passRate < 100` treats contract probes as **all-or-nothing** rather than thresholded — one failed probe fails the whole run. The `!= null` guard (rather than a truthy check) is deliberate so an `aggregate` of exactly `0` still flows through `computeVerdict` instead of dropping to the tally fallback. Note **`injection` is counted as a gate failure but is not one of the two hard-FAIL overrides** here — only `pii` and `safety` short-circuit.

howItWorks.step: Walks every prompt-level result to localize failures — which gate tripped, which metric scored low, which prompt IDs are the worst offenders — and emits one severity-tagged recommendation per pattern, naming the responsible prompts.
howItWorks.explain: Each recommendation is **localized** — it re-filters `promptResults` down to the exact prompts whose `gates.pii.passed === false` (a strict equality check, so `undefined`/skipped gates are excluded rather than lumped in as failures) and names them. The `[CRITICAL - PII]` prefix isn't cosmetic: it's the **severity tag the caller sorts on**, which is what floats gate leaks above per-metric weak-spots in the final list. `piiPrompts.slice(0, 5)` caps the named IDs so a run where dozens trip still produces a readable line, and the `|| []` default lets a summary-only run still emit aggregate-driven recs. The remediation text is **concrete and actionable** (forbid, redact, add provoking tests) rather than a generic 'investigate'.

howItWorks.step: Serializes the scorecard to multiple formats: JSON for downstream tooling, a human-readable Markdown report, and optional `.docx`/`.xlsx` for stakeholders who want a printable or spreadsheet view.
howItWorks.explain: Emits **plain Markdown, not HTML** — no template engine, no rendering dependency — so the scorecard opens identically in GitHub, any editor, or a downstream `.docx`/`.xlsx` converter. The `vb` helper maps a verdict to a badge label with a **fail-safe else branch**: anything that isn't `PASS` or `WARNING` collapses to `FAIL`, so a malformed verdict degrades toward caution rather than a false green. The timestamp is stored as ISO but rendered with `toLocaleString()` so it reads in the **viewer's** locale and timezone, and the layout leads with the executive-summary table so the **single overall verdict is the first thing a stakeholder sees**, ahead of any per-pipeline breakdown.

examples.caption: PII gate trips on a quality run
examples.input: Quality-grading results where 2 of 40 responses leaked a person's private information (`gateFails.pii === 2`).
examples.output: Overall verdict FAIL (gate override), a `[CRITICAL - PII]` line naming the affected prompt IDs, and three concrete actions: forbid it in the instructions, add a redaction step, and add tests that try to provoke it.

examples.caption: Clean run across both pipelines
examples.input: Contract probes at 100% pass rate and quality aggregate comfortably above the verdict threshold.
examples.output: Overall PASS, a note that all guardrails held on every prompt, and a recommendation to expand the dataset to hold confidence as the assistant changes.

examples.caption: A batch of WARNING-band answers
examples.input: Quality grades with several responses in the WARNING band, just under the pass threshold.
examples.output: Overall WARNING, the list of near-miss prompt IDs, and guidance on which metric improvements would flip the most of them to PASS.

underHood.heading: Discover latest result files
underHood.input: The two output directories — one holding contract/probe runs, one holding quality-grading runs.
underHood.output: The newest file in each directory, selected by `mtimeMs` (via `discoverLatestFile()`).

underHood.heading: Load and normalize both pipelines
underHood.whenRuns: Immediately after the latest files are located.
underHood.input: The two raw result files, shaped differently because they come from different pipelines.
underHood.output: One `EvalReportSummary` shape — pass rate, verdict counts, gate failures, average scores — independent of source pipeline (via `loadSystemResults()`, `loadUserResults()`, and `buildSummary()`).

underHood.heading: Compute overall verdict
underHood.whenRuns: Once both pipelines are normalized into the summary.
underHood.output: One overall PASS/WARNING/FAIL, decided by fixed precedence — any PII or safety gate failure forces FAIL regardless of other scores (via `computeOverallVerdict()`).

underHood.heading: Localize weak spots
underHood.whenRuns: After the overall verdict is set.
underHood.input: Every prompt-level result across the contract probes and the quality dimensions.
underHood.output: A severity-ranked list of the worst gates, metrics, and prompt IDs, each rendered as a recommendation with a concrete remediation (via `buildRecommendations()`).

underHood.heading: Serialize the scorecard
underHood.whenRuns: Last, once summary and recommendations are final.
underHood.input: The merged summary plus the recommendation list.
underHood.output: A JSON file for downstream tooling, a Markdown report, and — on request — a `.docx` and `.xlsx` for stakeholders (via `generateReportMarkdown()`, `generateWordDoc()`, and `generateExcel()`).

prerequisites: Node ≥ 18 and a terminal (macOS/Linux shell or Windows PowerShell).
At least one upstream pipeline already run: the contract/probe checks and/or the quality-grading run.
Nothing else to configure — this agent only reads result files other agents wrote; it never calls the assistant or an LLM judge itself.

steps.label: Install Node.js — the runtime for the agent.
steps.cmd:
# macOS (with Homebrew):
brew install node

# or download the LTS installer from nodejs.org, then check it worked:
node -v   # should print v18 or higher
steps.why: The agent is a TypeScript program; Node executes it. One-time per machine.
steps.firstRun: Needed only the first time on a new machine.

steps.label: Clone the agents and install dependencies.
steps.why: `npm install` pulls the agent's dependencies — the `.xlsx` writer and the `.docx` writer — into `node_modules`.
steps.rerun: No-op unless the dependency list changed.

steps.label: Ensure at least one upstream pipeline has produced a result file.
steps.cmd:
# Contract/probe checks:
npm run eval:contract:teacher && npm run eval:probe:teacher

# Quality grading:
npm run eval:user:run
steps.why: This agent tests nothing itself — it merges whatever the two upstream pipelines most recently wrote. With neither ever run, there is nothing to merge; it reports that and exits.

steps.label: Generate the scorecard.
steps.why: Discovers the newest file from each pipeline, normalizes and merges them, applies the fixed pass/warning/fail precedence, and writes the recommendations. `--word` adds a `.docx`; `--include-all` includes every prompt-level detail, not just the summary.
steps.firstRun: Reads whatever the latest runs of both pipelines produced.
steps.rerun: Re-run whenever either pipeline writes a new result file — it always picks the newest by mtime automatically.

steps.label: Open the generated scorecard.
steps.why: The `.md` is the scorecard — the overall PASS/WARNING/FAIL verdict, a section per pipeline, and the ranked list of what to fix and why.

inputs.name: --system-only | --user-only
inputs.desc: Scope the scorecard to only the contract/probe results, or only the quality results (default: both).

inputs.name: --word, --excel, --include-all
inputs.desc: Also emit a `.docx`, a `.xlsx`, or include every prompt-level detail rather than just the summary.

inputs.name: --filter-verdict <PASS,WARNING,FAIL>
inputs.desc: Include only prompts whose individual verdict is in this comma-separated set.

inputs.name: --system-path, --user-path, --comparison-path, --output <dir>
inputs.desc: Override which specific result file(s) to read, or the output directory, instead of auto-discovering the newest.

outputs.name: eval-report-<timestamp>.json / .md
outputs.desc: The structured and human-readable scorecard — overall verdict, per-pipeline summary, and ranked recommendations.

outputs.name: eval-report-<timestamp>.docx / .xlsx (optional)
outputs.desc: A `.docx` and/or `.xlsx` view, emitted only with `--word` or `--excel`.

runbook.rerun: Nothing to fingerprint — every run re-reads whichever result files have the newest mtime at that moment. Run it again right after a fresh probe or grading run and the scorecard reflects the latest numbers; nothing needs clearing first.
runbook.integrate: Chain it as the final CI step after the full eval pipeline (contract probes, then quality grading, then this), so every model or prompt change emits a fresh go/no-go scorecard with no hand-assembly.

video.caption: 2–3 min screen recording: run both upstream eval pipelines, then watch this agent discover and merge them into one scorecard.
script: Open a terminal and say: 'This agent gathers the scattered scores from testing the AI assistant's quality and safety into one clear scorecard.'
Run `node -v` to confirm Node is installed; say one line about what Node is.
Run `npm install` (or note it's already done); explain it's grabbing the helper libraries.
Briefly run (or point at recent output from) the rule-obedience probe checks and the answer-quality grading run — say 'these two piles are what gets merged.'
Run `npm run eval:report -- --word --include-all`; narrate as it finds the latest file from each pile.
Open the produced `.md` scorecard; point at the single overall verdict at the top.
Scroll to a recommendation, e.g. a flagged personal-data leak, and read the specific prompts it names.
Show the `--word` document it also generated, ready to hand to a non-technical stakeholder.
Close: 'One bad answer can sink trust in the whole assistant — this is what keeps a launch honest.'
